extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, and NIH/academic stakeholders studying NIH grant funding disparities
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of biosketch-, publication-, training-, and institution-level variables that predict NIH R01 award probability and explain race/ethnicity funding gaps. Focuses on bibliometrics, prior grants, training, and review-process outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH peer review criterion: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance — Does the project address an important problem?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the set of criterion reviewers evaluate (along with Innovation, Approach, Investigators, Environment). Under current NIH review, criterion scores are given initially (1–9) and correlate with overall impact scores; significance is one dimension considered when assigning preliminary and overall impact/priority scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH peer review criterion: Innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation — Does the project use novel concepts?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a standard NIH review criterion. Innovation is scored alongside Significance, Approach, Investigators, and Environment and influences preliminary criterion scores and overall impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH peer review criterion: Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach — Are the methods rigorous?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A core NIH review criterion assessing the rigor and feasibility of proposed methods; influences criterion scores and overall impact. The paper notes reviewers evaluate approach, significance, innovation, investigator, and environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH peer review criterion: Investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators — Are the PIs and team well qualified?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluated as part of NIH criterion scores; includes assessment of investigator track record (publications, prior funding, training) often reflected in the biosketch and bibliometric measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH peer review criterion: Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Environment — Will the institutional setting contribute to success?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessed in NIH review; proxied empirically here by NIH funding rank of the employer and other institutional prestige measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall impact / priority score (score vs no score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications receive preliminary criterion scores; the most meritorious (~half) are discussed and given a final priority/overall impact score; receiving a score vs getting no score (score/no-score decision) is an important determinant of funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper separates the black/white funding gap into (1) probability of receiving a priority/impact score and (2) conditional probability of funding given a score; it emphasizes that significant unexplained differences involve the score/no-score decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application components considered
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIH application consists of the research plan, the biosketches of key personnel, and the budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study treats information available at time of review (including biosketch-listed publications and associated bibliometrics) as explanatory covariates for award probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of publications reported on Biosketch
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of peer‑reviewed publications listed on the applicant's NIH Biosketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biosketch data showed an average of 22.5 publications per investigator in the sample; name-matching undercounts publications, so Biosketch-reported counts better reflect what reviewers see.

rubrics_metrics.name: Log of sum of journal impact factors (bibliometric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural logarithm of the sum of the journal impact factors for all the applicant’s publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as an optimal bibliometric measure in this study; a 1% increase in the sum is associated with a 6.7 percentage-point increase in funding probability. Natural log used to improve model fit due to skewed distributions. Use is controversial but reviewers appear to use journal impact as a proxy for quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage of first‑authored publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Share of the applicant's publications where the applicant is first author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher percentage of first-authorship is positively associated with award probability (e.g., 1% increase associated with 9.1 ppt increase in probability in one model). Included among bibliometric explanatory variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage of last‑authored publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Share of the applicant's publications where the applicant is last (senior) author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an indicator of leading contributions/independence; one of the bibliometric measures entered into models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage of papers in top quartile of field (field‑normalized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage of an applicant's publications ranked in the top quartile of citations relative to papers in the same Web of Science journal subject category over the first two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field-normalized measure to account for differing citation patterns across fields; higher values reduce the black/white gap and are positively associated with funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage of uncited papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Share of publications that received zero citations (within the two-year window used for field-normalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher percentage of uncited papers is negatively associated with award probability and helps explain part of funding differentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage of top three coauthors' papers in top quartile
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage of the publications by the applicant’s top three coauthors that lie in the top quartile of the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a proxy for strength/reach of professional networks; coauthors' high-impact publications are positively associated with the applicant’s award probability though they did not fully close the race gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-normalization method for bibliometrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations to a given publication over the first two years are compared to citations to papers in the same Web of Science journal subject category during the same two years to assign a field-normalized quartile rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to adjust for different publication/citation norms across fields; central to deriving percentages in top quartiles and top 10% measures used in models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations (raw counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of times an applicant's publications have been cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in earlier studies, but journal impact factor–based measures (sum of JIFs) provided better explanatory power here because journals are visible on the Biosketch and reviewers may use impact factor as proxy; citation distributions are highly skewed and log transforms are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author position and coauthor count
rubrics_metrics.description: Author position on each paper (first, last, middle) and number of coauthors per paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to allocate publications to career stages and as covariates (e.g., percent first/last authored, number of coauthors) that influence award probability; coauthor count differences observed by race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proxy measures of professional networks (last authors and frequent coauthors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying the three most frequent last authors and three most frequent coauthors on an applicant’s papers and constructing bibliometric measures from their publication records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures serve as proxies for the professional networks of applicants and are used to examine network effects on funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior NIH grants and Type 2 (renewal) awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of prior NIH grants by funding mechanism, and number of prior R01 Type 2 (competing renewal) awards held by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior NIH grants are important explanatory variables; each additional Type 2 award increased probability of receiving a new Type 1 R01 (e.g., ~2 ppt); inclusion of improved measures of prior NIH funding explains a substantial portion of the black/white gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior non‑NIH grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of prior non-NIH federal grants, foundation grants, private sources, and international grants reported on the Biosketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study non-NIH grants had no significant effect on R01 award probability in contrast to prior NIH grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH funding rank of employer institution
rubrics_metrics.description: An NIH funding-based rank of the undergraduate/PhD/postdoctoral and employing institutions used as a proxy for research intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher NIH funding rank is associated with higher award probability and explains part of the race/ethnicity gap; institutions partitioned into Top 100 vs 101+ for subgroup analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic rank at time of application
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant's academic rank (e.g., assistant, associate, full professor) when the application was submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full professor increased probability of NIH funding (e.g., ~11.9 ppt in one specification), but the black/white gap remained; academic rank is included as an explanatory covariate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and training history (undergraduate, PhD, postdoc institutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Undergraduate, PhD, and postdoctoral institutions, fellowships, traineeships, and grants listed on the Biosketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to proxy institutional prestige and selectivity (linked to IPEDS, Carnegie Classification, Oberlin Group); training variables were largely exogenous but did not appreciably reduce the black/white funding gap relative to bibliometrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predoctoral and postdoctoral fellowships and traineeships
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of predoctoral/postdoctoral fellowships (F31, F32, T32), traineeships, and diversity-related fellowships listed on Biosketches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in models of training; useful to examine NIH training effects but had limited explanatory power compared to publication bibliometrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of PhD/postdoctoral advisors (where available)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempted identification of advisors (via last-author matching) to control for mentorship, but found few Biosketches list advisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because advisor identification was incomplete (only 56% match in subset), the analysis could not effectively control for advisor effects; this is noted as a limitation in controlling for mentorship influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation on review/advisory panels and professional service
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of advisory panels, professional society memberships, and leadership positions reported on the Biosketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participating on NIH review panels is positively associated with award probability (especially for experienced investigators), while participating on non-NIH review panels had a negative and significant association (-3.6 ppt). Reviewer/committee experience included as explanatory covariate.

rubrics_metrics.name: New vs Experienced investigator status
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorization of applicants as New Investigators (never received R01/R01-equivalent) vs Experienced Investigators (eligible for Type 2 renewals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH policy and empirical differences motivate separate analyses; determinants of funding differ across these groups and the black/white gap varies by experience status (different magnitudes and significance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree type subgrouping (PhD, MD, MD/PhD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partitioning applicants by degree type (PhD, MD, MD/PhD) to examine differential effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MDs and MD/PhDs showed smaller black/white funding gaps than PhDs in previous analyses; degree type affects publication patterns and may influence reviewers' assessments (e.g., clinical duties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of publications / career-stage assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning each publication to career stages (undergraduate, graduate, postdoc, independent) using degree dates and postdoctoral appointment dates to examine when career divergence by race occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show divergence may begin as early as the postdoc; suggests interventions should focus on early-career mentoring and timing-of-publication patterns are informative for evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name-matched vs Biosketch-based publication measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of publication/citation counts derived from name-matching algorithms versus those reported on the Biosketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name-matching undercounts publications and explains less of the race gap; Biosketch-based measures (including sum of JIFs) provide better explanatory power because journals are visible to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission controls and robustness checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlling for proposal resubmissions and conducting robustness tests across subgroups (new vs experienced, degree types, institution rank).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to check stability of main findings; resubmission status was included in supplementary specifications (e.g., Fig C) to understand its effect on predicted probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling choices and interpretation (probit, marginal effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of probit models to analyze probability of receiving an R01 award and reporting marginal effects of race/ethnicity relative to whites rather than probit coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimates are correlations, not causal effects. Multiple specifications are estimated because many covariates are endogenous. P-values adjusted for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni correction; linear probability models and Gelbach decomposition used to quantify contributions of covariates to explained gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Log transformation for skewed bibliometrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply natural log transforms to bibliometric measures (e.g., sum of impact factors) to improve model fit due to skewed citation and impact-factor distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper explicitly uses the log of sums because citation and impact distributions are highly skewed and the log transform stabilizes variance and model fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: Use of journal impact factor (JIF) as proxy
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning that using journal impact factor to evaluate individual publications is controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes the controversy (citations to San Francisco Declaration and other critiques) but also that reviewers likely use familiarity with impact factors as a proxy; authors employ JIF-based measures while acknowledging limitations and skewness of citation distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant narrative / modified Biosketch (policy intervention)
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH piloted modified Biosketch allowing a narrative account of 'up to five of their most significant contributions to science'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested as a production guideline/intervention to 'level the Biosketch playing field' and potentially reduce reliance on raw publication counts/impact factors; considered a potential mitigating policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentoring intervention to increase publications and bibliometric quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfactual policy experiment simulating mentoring interventions that increase quantity and quality of publications for black investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to estimate potential impact on award probabilities; mentoring (conveying tacit knowledge about topic choice, grantsmanship, publication process) is recommended as an intervention and has precedent in randomized trials improving publications and grant acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion / privacy constraints on data sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-decisional grant application and personally identifiable information cannot be made public by law (Privacy Act); FOIA processes apply for funded grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits data availability for reproducing analyses and is noted as a procedural constraint impacting research transparency and data access.
